analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from firing or refusing to hire workers because they are gay or transgender.
analysis.headline: A bill to prohibit firing workers for being gay or transgender died in House committees without a vote, despite 206 cosponsors including 8 Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for employers with 15 or more workers, employment agencies, and unions to discriminate against someone for their actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity. It would have let workers sue, with the same procedures and remedies used for race and sex discrimination claims. It carved out religious organizations and the military, banned quotas, and barred the government from collecting statistics on workers' orientation or identity.
analysis.who_benefits: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender workers — and anyone fired for associating with LGBT people — who in states without their own nondiscrimination laws could be fired, denied a job, or paid less with no federal recourse. The bill gave them the same complaint, investigation, and court remedies already available for race or sex discrimination.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice for an employer with 15 or more employees to fire, refuse to hire, or discriminate against a worker because of actual or perceived sexual orientation or gender identity [S3].

Gives the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the Attorney General, and federal courts the same enforcement powers and remedies they have under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and bars retaliation against workers who file charges [S2].
Allows suits against state and federal government employers, waiving state immunity where states take federal money, with compensatory damages available though not punitive damages [S3].
Extends protection to association — an employer may not discriminate against a worker because of the sexual orientation or gender identity of someone the worker is associated with [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees face new compliance obligations and potential lawsuits, though the bill allows only disparate-treatment claims, permits reasonable dress codes, and requires no new facilities. Religious organizations are fully exempt, and the military relationship is excluded.

drawbacks.text: The religious exemption covers any organization exempt from Title VII's religious provisions, which includes many church-affiliated hospitals, schools, and charities — so millions of workers at those employers would have gotten no protection [S3].
The bill allows only disparate-treatment claims, so a worker could not challenge a policy that has a discriminatory effect without proof of intentional discrimination [S2].
Employers of fewer than 15 employees are outside the bill entirely, and remedies against the government exclude punitive damages, leaving some discrimination without a full remedy [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given roughly the same federal protection against anti-LGBT job discrimination that federal law already provides for race, sex, religion, and national origin, at a compliance and litigation cost to mid-size and large employers that is modest by the standards of existing civil-rights law. Its main weaknesses are the broad religious exemption and the ban on disparate-impact claims, which shrink who is covered. On balance it was a worker-protection bill with real limits, and it never received a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2013 and referred to four House committees; it was sent to two subcommittees that summer and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Polis introduced the Employment Non-Discrimination Act of 2013 on April 25, 2013, with an initial cosponsor list including Republican Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen and Democratic leaders such as Nancy Pelosi and Steny Hoyer [S3].

The bill was referred to four committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary — meaning any one of them could have kept it from advancing [S5].

In June and July 2013 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Workforce Protections; no markup or vote is recorded afterward, and no further action appears in the Congress [S5].
The bill finished the 113th Congress with 206 cosponsors, 198 Democrats and 8 Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: House leadership and committee chairs who declined to advance the bill kept the status quo, and employers in states without their own nondiscrimination laws could continue firing LGBT workers with no federal recourse.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: House leaders who never scheduled it

for.name: Rep. Jared Polis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a large initial cosponsor list spanning both parties.

for.name: 198 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it majority-House support on paper.

for.name: 8 of 234 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, who was among its original sponsors.

against.name: John Boehner
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill — or the Senate-passed companion — for a House floor vote, despite its apparent majority support; publicly said he saw no need for the legislation.

against.name: House committee chairs
against.role: Chairs of Education and the Workforce, Judiciary, Oversight, and House Administration
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 198 of 233 Democrats cosponsored — with a small bipartisan fringe of 8 Republicans out of 234; no floor vote was ever held to test the full chamber.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed large employers to discrimination claims by LGBT workers, following the same enforcement machinery as race and sex discrimination cases. Its defeat left those employers free of that obligation, but workers in states without their own laws remained unprotected.

The bill exempts organizations covered by Title VII's religious-employer carve-outs, so religiously affiliated employers could continue making hiring decisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Had the bill passed without this carve-out, they would have faced the new rules.
